47	   and confirmed is about the same problem.

56	   issue names the package only inside pasted tool output.

58	   duplicate. Mention a real related issue as `#NNNN` in your comment, never as a URL
59	   (a URL to an upstream issue would post a cross-reference on it).

113	   tests styles and colours against Rich's own parser, so if it rejects one,
114	   the suggestion is wrong; change the advice, do not drop the check. Post the
115	   checked text unchanged.

1:.. _highlighting:
3:Highlighting
6:Rich will automatically highlight patterns in text, such as numbers, strings, collections, booleans, None, and a few more exotic patterns such as file paths, URLs and UUIDs.
8:You can disable highlighting either by setting ``highlight=False`` on :meth:`~rich.console.Console.print` or :meth:`~rich.console.Console.log`, or by setting ``highlight=False`` on the :class:`~rich.console.Console` constructor which disables it everywhere. If you disable highlighting on the constructor, you can still selectively *enable* highlighting with ``highlight=True`` on print / log.
10:Custom Highlighters
13:If the default highlighting doesn't fit your needs, you can define a custom highlighter. The easiest way to do this is to extend the :class:`~rich.highlighter.RegexHighlighter` class which applies a style to any text matching a list of regular expressions.
15:Here's an example which highlights text that looks like an email address::
18:    from rich.highlighter import RegexHighlighter
21:    class EmailHighlighter(RegexHighlighter):
25:        highlights = [r"(?P<email>[\w-]+@([\w-]+\.)+[\w-]+)"]
29:    console = Console(highlighter=EmailHighlighter(), theme=theme)
33:The ``highlights`` class variable should contain a list of regular expressions. The group names of any matching expressions are prefixed with the ``base_style`` attribute and used as styles for matching text. In the example above, any email addresses will have the style "example.email" applied, which we've defined in a custom :ref:`Theme <themes>`.
35:Setting the highlighter on the Console will apply highlighting to all text you print (if enabled). You can also use a highlighter on a more granular level by using the instance as a callable and printing the result. For example, we could use the email highlighter class like this::
39:    highlight_emails = EmailHighlighter()
40:    console.print(highlight_emails("Send funds to money@example.org"))
43:While :class:`~rich.highlighter.RegexHighlighter` is quite powerful, you can also extend its base class :class:`~rich.highlighter.Highlighter` to implement a custom scheme for highlighting. It contains a single method :class:`~rich.highlighter.Highlighter.highlight` which is passed the :class:`~rich.text.Text` to highlight.
45:Here's a silly example that highlights every character with a different color::
50:    from rich.highlighter import Highlighter
53:    class RainbowHighlighter(Highlighter):
54:        def highlight(self, text):
59:    rainbow = RainbowHighlighter()
62:Builtin Highlighters
65:The following builtin highlighters are available.
67:* :class:`~rich.highlighter.ISO8601Highlighter` Highlights ISO8601 date time strings.
68:* :class:`~rich.highlighter.JSONHighlighter` Highlights JSON formatted strings.

- **Label:** `enhancement`. Rich has no built-in unit styling, and adding it needs new code in `ReprHighlighter`.
- **Comment:** asks the reporter to start in Discussions, since features need approval there first. It points to the custom `RegexHighlighter` route in the highlighting docs, and mentions #3318 as a related open report on the same number regex.
- **Duplicates:** none. The closest hits (#3522, #3854, #2299, #3075) are different problems, so I did not mark it `duplicate`.
- **Checks:** the author is `NONE`, so this is not a maintainer issue. `validate_labels.py` returned `ok: true`. `check_comment.py` first flagged a trailing full stop being read as part of the docs link; I reworded so the link stands alone, and it then passed.
